lesson.title: Monkey Business in Dayton: The Scopes Trial
lesson.summary: The 1925 trial of teacher John Scopes in Dayton, Tennessee, pitted the legacy of religious revivalism against the scientific ambitions of the Progressive Era, becoming a national media spectacle over whether evolution could be taught in public schools.
lesson.body:
In March 1925, the Tennessee state legislature passed the Butler Act, a law that made it illegal for any public school teacher in the state to teach any theory that denied the biblical account of divine creation, effectively banning the teaching of human evolution. The law reflected a strain of Protestant religious conviction with deep roots in American history, stretching back through generations of revivalist preaching that had periodically swept the country since the Great Awakening of the colonial era, and which by the 1920s had crystallized into a modern fundamentalist movement determined to defend a literal reading of the Bible against the perceived threats of modern science and secular culture.

The American Civil Liberties Union, looking for a case to challenge the law's constitutionality, advertised for a Tennessee teacher willing to be prosecuted as a test case. In the small town of Dayton, local boosters saw an opportunity to bring publicity and business to their community, and John T. Scopes, a young high school teacher and football coach, agreed to be charged with violating the Butler Act. The resulting trial in July 1925 became a national sensation. William Jennings Bryan, a three time presidential candidate and former Secretary of State famous for his devout Christian faith, joined the prosecution, while the legendary defense attorney Clarence Darrow, working with the ACLU, took up Scopes's defense. The scientific curriculum Scopes was accused of violating was itself partly a legacy of the Progressive Era, when reformers had pushed hard to expand and modernize public education, making the trial as much a clash between two eras of American reform as between science and religion.

The trial's most famous moment came when Darrow, unable to call scientific experts to testify on evolution under the judge's rulings, instead called Bryan himself to the stand as an expert on the Bible, and pressed him with pointed questions about whether every biblical story should be read literally. Reporters, including the sharp tongued journalist H.L. Mencken, covered the trial closely, and it was broadcast live on radio, one of the first trials to reach a national audience this way. In the end, the jury found Scopes guilty, and the judge fined him one hundred dollars, though the Tennessee Supreme Court later overturned the conviction on a legal technicality rather than on any constitutional grounds, and the Butler Act itself remained on the books for decades. William Jennings Bryan died just five days after the trial ended, exhausted from the ordeal. The Scopes Trial did not settle the underlying argument over evolution and religion in American public life, a debate that in many forms continues today, but it captured, in a single small town courtroom, the deep cultural divide between rural traditionalism and modern science that ran through the entire decade.
